taskflow.title: TaskFlow
taskflow.summary: A team project and task manager with a REST API of its own: workspaces, roles, a drag-and-drop board and real time.
taskflow.imageAlt: Kanban board of a project in TaskFlow.
description: A team project and task management application, in three levels — workspaces, projects and tasks — with members and roles. Every task has a status, a priority, a due date, an assignee, comments with mentions and a history, and moves between columns by being dragged across the board.

The API lives in its own repository: Express 5 and TypeScript in layers (route → controller → service → repository), Prisma on top of PostgreSQL, Zod validating everything that comes in, and sessions with access and refresh JWTs in httpOnly cookies. Its 378 tests are integration tests: they hit the real API against its own Postgres in Docker.

The history and the notifications are not solved separately: they come out of a single event table, written in the same transaction as the change that caused it, so the log cannot claim something that later rolled back. Avatars never go through the API: the browser compresses the image, asks for a signed URL and uploads the file straight to the bucket — Cloudflare R2 in production, MinIO locally — and the backend only confirms afterwards that the object is there. And card ordering uses lexorank, the way Jira does it, because a numeric field runs out of room as you reorder.

The client is Next.js 16 with the App Router and React 19: React Query for server state and optimistic dragging, socket.io for real time, and filters, search and pagination in the URL through nuqs, so any view can be shared as a link. It is my largest project so far, and the first where I wrote the decisions down as I made them.
shots: A workspace summary: the counters, the projects, my own queue of tasks and the activity log. A counter only counts reachable work — active projects you belong to, and the tasks inside them — because a number larger than the list right below it reads as a bug, not as extra information. And the feed cuts one level below its scope: it reaches the projects, never each task's detail, because a single busy project would drown out the rest.

A project summary, with its tasks by status, by priority and by due date. Charts live only here: it is the one scope with enough homogeneous data for a chart to mean anything, so the workspace summary deliberately has none. Due dates go into buckets — overdue, this week, scheduled, no date — and "overdue" means its day has already passed in the user's own time zone: what is due today does not count until tomorrow.

The task list, with its filters for status, priority, date, archived and favourites. Filters, search, sorting, page and the open tab live in the URL through nuqs, never in useState: a link to "the archived tasks" has to open right there and survive a refresh.

Task detail: its fields, the comment thread with mentions, and the activity. The modal is mounted once at the root and addressed through the URL, so it opens the same way from the list, the board or the search, without losing the screen behind it. Mentions go by username and the comment stores the id alongside it: the id is the only immutable part, and the username keeps the text readable if that person is no longer on the project. Editing only notifies whoever the edit mentions for the first time, because fixing a typo should not ring anyone's bell.

A workspace's members and their roles, with pending and inactive ones behind a filter of their own. Nobody is deleted: every removal is a soft one and each has its inverse verb, but it wipes the role, so coming back asks which role to return with instead of storing a previous one that goes stale. That filter is only drawn for whoever can undo the removal, because showing rows that lead nowhere is a dead end, and when a row has a single action it is a button: a one-item menu makes you open it to find out there was nothing to choose.

Global search, opened with ⌘K from any screen. It crosses workspaces, projects and tasks in a single request and resolves no slug, so the only thing separating yours from everyone else's is the same visibility predicate the summaries use: what you cannot open from any screen cannot surface here either. It also searches by the task's label, WEB-12, which exists in no column: it has to be split into the project key and the number.

graphly.title: Graphly
graphly.summary: A tool to create personal metrics, log entries and explore them in interactive charts from a single dashboard.
description: A personal data visualisation tool for creating metrics, logging entries and exploring the data through interactive charts.

Built with Next.js and Server Actions to keep frontend and backend in a single project. Clerk handles authentication, Drizzle ORM and Neon provide typed access to the database, and Shadcn/UI speeds up building the interface.

gruas-y-transportes-ryp.title: Grúas y transportes RYP
gruas-y-transportes-ryp.summary: Corporate website for a self-loading crane and haulage company, built to bring in quote requests.
gruas-y-transportes-ryp.imageAlt: Home page of the Grúas y transportes RYP website.
description: Corporate website for a self-loading crane and haulage company in Valencia. It presents the services, explains the booking process in three steps and collects quote requests through a form.

Getting in touch is always one tap away: a landline in the header, a floating WhatsApp button on every page, and a form covering the type of service and a description of the job. It also includes a language switcher and an accessibility widget.

One of several client websites I built during my internship at Grup Apunts. Made with WordPress for a quick turnaround and a site the client can maintain on their own, then tuned for search so they get found by the services they offer.
shots: The "About us" page, introducing the company.
The booking process, explained in three steps.
Contact page, with the quote form and the company details.

solar.title: Solar
solar.summary: An application to manage power generation plants and keep track of their production and consumption.
description: Web application for managing power generation plants. Each plant stores its installed capacity, coordinates, an image and its status, and builds up production and consumption records that the application sums up in charts and in a balance per period.

Built with Angular because it had to run entirely on the client, Tailwind CSS to keep the interface modular and maintainable, and Supabase as a Backend as a Service (BaaS), which removed the need to build and maintain a backend of my own.
It was my final project for the Web Application Development programme, and the first one I designed end to end by myself: data model, interface and deployment.
shots: Plants listed in a table, with their capacity, location and status, plus the filtering and sorting controls.

Logging form, with production, consumption and an optional note.
Records table, with the balance of each one and the chart for the period.

experience.title: Grup Apunts
experience.description: I implemented new features in web applications with Symfony and brought some of them to mobile with Flutter. Working between the custom development team and the digital marketing one, I also built corporate websites and online stores with WordPress, tailored to what each client needed, and took care of maintenance and SEO for the sites of companies and local businesses.

experience.title: AELE, Armarios Levante
experience.description: I built the company's web quoting tool with React: I integrated the catalogue with all of its combinations and added the wardrobe calculation and customisation tools to speed up quoting and improve the customer experience. I also took it all the way to production.

bio: I'm Óscar Esteve, a full-stack developer based in Alzira, Valencia. I got into development wanting to understand how the things I used every day actually worked, and that curiosity led me through the SMR, DAM and DAW programmes.

I work on web applications end to end: I've implemented features with Symfony, built a quoting tool with React and integrated the company catalogue into it, and created corporate websites and online stores with WordPress. Frontend is where I'm most at home, putting together clean interfaces that are easy to use.

I keep building my own projects because I like to carry on learning on my own: when a technology catches my attention, I build something with it until I properly understand how it works. The latest one is TaskFlow, where I took on both halves: a REST API in Express with roles, domain events and integration tests, and its Next.js client with a drag-and-drop board and real-time updates.
